title: Before anaesthesia, 90 seconds was considered a good time for an amputation
body: Pain during surgery could send patients into shock, so surgeons prided themselves on speed. That changed on **16 October 1846** in the operating theatre of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. The dentist William Morton had a young printer, Edward Gilbert Abbott, breathe ether vapour, and the surgeon John Collins Warren then painlessly removed part of a tumour from his neck. It was the first public demonstration of ether as a surgical anaesthetic, and the room is now known as the **Ether Dome**.

cover.alt: Inside the Ether Dome, a round 19th-century operating theatre with steep curved rows of blue seats under a white domed ceiling

slides.prompt: In Boston in 1846, dentist William Morton gave printer Edward Gilbert Abbott ether before surgery. What did Abbott say on waking?
slides.answer: "Feels as if my neck's been scratched"
slides.detail: The operation to remove part of a tumour from his neck had been painless.

slides.attribution: Surgeon John Collins Warren, turning to the observers, 16 October 1846

slides.alt: A painting of a crowd of men in dark 19th-century suits gathered around a patient lying unconscious in a chair in an operating theatre
slides.caption: Robert C. Hinckley's painting Ether Day, or The First Operation with Ether, recreating the scene in the operating theatre now called the Ether Dome.

slides.question: Ether Day was the first public demonstration. Who had already used ether in an operation, back in 1842?
slides.explanation: Crawford Long removed a tumour from a young man's neck under ether in 1842, but he did not publish anything until he read about Morton's demonstration.

slides.heading: The race to painless surgery
slides.note: Wells's 1845 nitrous oxide demonstration was dismissed as humbug when his patient cried out

slides.heading: Why it changed surgery
slides.text: With the patient unconscious, a surgeon no longer had to race against pain and shock. Warren could take his time over a delicate operation that speed surgery did not allow. By December 1846 a medical journal was already reporting on Morton's demonstration.
